content.text: I am trying to make a bmw ride planner which is made for motorcycle riders so the thing is that it’s more about the experience during the ride than getting from point a to point b. And to help with this I have a dataset given by bmw themselves to help make this ride planner so I want you to come up with a full proper plan for making this app from how this app will work all the answers to the questions and how the ui will look, the tech stack, how can we optimize this for the demo pitch so it works live during the demo all those sort of things. And I will also upload more pictures so wait until I upload the other pics to make the plan

Got all four pages. Holding off on the plan until you've uploaded the rest.

Here's what I've captured so far so you know nothing's lost:

**Page 1 (the framing questions)** — What data is used ①, how is that data used, how will we visualize it in the backend, how will we make the UI for demo purposes. Plus "destination + or joy ride" as a mode distinction.

**Page 2 — What data is used:** speed, location, type of bike ("everything in the dataset"), road conditions, weather, rider information (age, preferences, previous rides — pulled from profile), road profile, traffic info.

**Page 3 — How the data is used:** rider preference inferred from weather / road type / speeds / bike type / rider profile; find a scenic route with curves, aspects riders consider fun, traffic, weather.

**Page 4 — UI for demo:** weather API, traffic API, scenic spots on the way, type of bike you ride, lean angles, and the option to *preview/view the ride before you even go on it*.

Two things that would help me write a plan that's actually grounded rather than generic — feel free to send them alongside the next photos:

1. **The BMW dataset itself** — schema, a sample, or even just the column names and roughly how many rows/rides. Whether it's per-ride telemetry, aggregated stats, or fleet-level changes the architecture a lot (especially whether "lean angles" and "fun roads" can be *derived from real data* or have to be heuristics).
2. **Constraints** — how long until the pitch, and who's building what (memory says main/dev/feat for you, Niko, and Alex on `krishaanth5831/BMW-Ride-Planner`).

Send the rest of the pics whenever you're ready and I'll put the full plan together.

hackathon (context given 2026-09-12). The premise: routing for motorcyclists
optimises for *enjoyment of the ride* — corners, elevation, scenery, stops —
not shortest A-to-B time. Judge-facing.

as collaborators.

checks — a required check that never reports would make every PR unmergeable.

user's instruction (2026-09-12)** — they want workflow docs and branching
conventions settled only once the stack is picked, not before. It is recoverable
from git history if wanted. The branches and protection were left in place; only
the doc went.

process scaffolding as premature. Don't re-propose workflow docs, CI, or

result.output: === tripViewer README === # ConnectedRide Trips Viewer A small web app that plots transpformed recorded motorcycle rides on a map. It reads CSV track data and shows single rides, heatmaps across all rides, and averaged "Morton cells". It is a playground to visualize data and to find patterns. > **Quick & dirty tool.** This viewer was put together to help you get quickly > familiar with the trip data offered for the Hackathon. It is not > production-quality code and not the expected starting point for any real > implementation. ## Requirements - **Python 3** – used to serve the files locally (no packages to install). - **A modern web browser** – Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari (recent version). - **Internet access** – map tiles and the Leaflet library load from the web. - No build step or extra dependencies are needed. ## Run ```bash cd web python3 -m http.server 8765 ``` Then open http://localhost:8765/. ## Controls ### Data source - **Choose files** – load one or more `.csv` ride files from your computer. - **Choose folder** – load every `.csv` file found in a folder, scanning all of its subfolders too (non-CSV files encountered there are skipped). - **Reload bundled data** – load the demo dataset that ships with the app. ### View mode - **Single ride** – draw one ride as a colored line. - **Heatmap (all rides)** – draw every ride, colored by a chosen metric. - **Morton cells (avg)** – split the map into `morton_code` cells and fill each cell with the average of a chosen metric. ### Map style - **Style 1** – normal map tiles. - **Black/White** – grayscale map tiles. - **No map** – hide the background map (tracks only). ### Morton grid - **Show grid overlay** – draw the `morton_code` cell boundaries. - **Show cell morton codes** – print each cell's `morton_code` in its top-left corner (only when few enough cells are visible). - **Level slider** – how fine the grid is. Higher = smaller cells / longer codes. ### Ride - **Ride dropdown** – pick which ride to show in Single-ride mode. ### Single-ride options (Single ride mode) - **Color track by** – Engine speed (RPM), Riding speed, Lean angle, or a solid color. - **Verbose mode** – show all CSV fields in the hover tooltip (needs raw data). - **ABS events / ASC events** – mark points where ABS/ASC activated. ### Heat aspect (Heatmap & Morton cells modes) Choose what the color represents: rides density, max/avg engine speed, max/avg lean angle, max/avg riding speed, curviness, or fun factor. ### Cell size (Heatmap mode) - **Cell size slider** – how coarse the heatmap binning is. ### Legend - Shows the color scale. input.content:
# BMW Ride Planner — Build & Pitch Plan

## Context

BMW Motorrad's track at the TUM.ai Zurich hackathon ("FIND YOUR THRILL — Route
Challenge") asks for a route planner for motorcyclists where the objective is
the *quality of the ride*, not the trip time. We have BMW's dataset on disk and
pitch **tomorrow morning (~09:00–11:00)** — roughly 16 working hours from now.

The brief (`~/Desktop/BMW/20260912 Hackathon Presentation Zürich Short 2.pdf`,
p.2) states the evaluation metrics verbatim. Everything below is organised
against them:

| # | Rubric metric | Where this plan delivers it |
|---|---------------|------------------------------|
| 1 | Usage of BMW **Crowd Data** | 85,699-trip aggregate → the routing graph itself |
| 2 | Usage of BMW **Personal Rider Data** | Revealed-preference weight fitting per rider |
| 3 | Usage of **External Sources** | Open-Meteo weather + OSM scenic POIs |
| 4 | **Scalability & Efficiency** | Morton-prefix precompute: 13 GB → ~30 MB served |
| 5 | Calculation of **Fun Score** | Normalised per-km feature score, explainable on stage |
| 6 | Consideration of **Rider Safety** | Crowd ABS rate + personal lean-capability matching |

Deliverables they name: the exact definition of "good route", an overview of all
data sources and their weighting, a visual route-planning tool, and a live demo
with an algorithm walk-through ("explainability + live demo score bonus points").

### One concern, stated once

You chose **both** use cases at equal weight. In 16 hours that is only feasible
because the joy-ride loop is built as a thin wrapper over the *same* graph, the
*same* scorer and the *same* Dijkstra as A→B — no second engine. The hard rule:
if Milestone 2 (personalised A→B, explainable) is not green by **00:30**, the
loop gets cut and must not appear on a slide. Do not promise on stage what isn't
running on the laptop.

---

## What the data actually contains (verified, not assumed)

`~/Desktop/BMW/exd_download/datasetHackathon/`

- **`anonymizedDataLake/trips-samples-{1,2}/{00..ff}/*.csv`** — **85,699 trips**,
  13 GB, sharded by morton-code prefix. 42 columns, ~1 Hz sampling, median ~310
  rows (~5 min snippets). This is the crowd corpus.
- **`exampleUser{A,B,C}/recordedTrips/*.csv`** — 101 / 73 / 224 full trips (userA
  up to 17,702 rows ≈ 5 h). Same schema. These are the three personal riders.
- **`exampleUserA/plannedRoutes/*.gpx`** — 89 routes the rider *planned in the
  BMW app*, carrying BMW's own option vocabulary:
  `<cnrd:routeOptions optimization="winding|fastest" windingness hilliness>` and
  `<cnrd:avoidances motorways dirtRoads alreadyUsedRoads .../>`.
- **`tripViewer/tripViewer/{app.js,index.html,style.css}`** — BMW's own Leaflet
  viewer. Read it; it is our frontend base and it hands us three things free:
  the **morton grid/heatmap layer**, the **ride playback with live lean/speed
  gauges**, and a documented `funFactor` we can beat.

### Column reality check — read this before writing any feature

Fill rates measured over 150 lake trips and all of userA/B/C:

| Column | Lake | userA | userB | userC | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sensorsbankingangle` | 100% | 89% | 83% | 100% | **The moat.** Backbone of everything. |
| `positionmapmatchedlat/lon` | 100% | 99% | — | — | Use for map-matched geometry |
| `positionrawelevation` | 100% | 99% | 100% | 100% | **Use this** for elevation |
| `positionmapmatchedelevation` | 46% | 70% | — | — | Too sparse — do not use |
| `ridingvehiclespeed` | 88% | 55% | 70% | 80% | Good; fall back to `positionrawspeed` |
| `ridingabsbraking` | 99% | 88% | 86% | 99% | Safety / road-condition signal |
| `ridingenginespeed` | 97% | 82% | — | — | Feeds fun score |
| `ridingthrottlevalue` | 73% | 64% | — | — | Usable with care |
| `sensorsaccelerationlongitudinal` | 99% | 78% | — | — | Braking proxy |
| `sensorsoutsidetemperature` | 94% | 88% | — | — | Historical weather proxy |
| `sensorsbreakpressurefront/rear` | **0%** | 0% | 0% | 0% | **Dead column — never touch it** |
| `sensorsaccelerationlateral` | 70% | **3%** | **5%** | 73% | Works on crowd, empty for 2 of 3 riders — **cannot be in the personal profile** |
| `trip_id` | 56% | 68% | — | — | Unreliable; **use the filename** as trip id |

Three corrections to the whiteboard notes, all of which a BMW engineer in the
room would catch:

1. **Braking is not in brake pressure.** It has to come from `ridingabsbraking`
   plus `sensorsaccelerationlongitudinal`.
2. **Rider age does not exist in this dataset.** Drop it. "Personal Rider Data"
   is a graded metric — claiming a field we don't have is the one thing that
   reads as fabrication. The profile is derived from riding behaviour only.
3. **Bike model is not in the dataset either.** Infer a coarse class
   (rpm-per-km/h ratio, gear count, lean envelope, tyre pressure) *and* let the
   user confirm it in a UI dropdown. Say "inferred, rider-confirmable" on stage.

### Geography — demo in Bavaria, not Zurich

Crowd data is concentrated at **47.6–48.5 N, 11.0–11.9 E** (Munich and its
southern foothills). userA's personal rides reach 43.6–48.9 N, 4.8–13.4 E (the
Alps, Dolomites, South Tyrol). Their own planned-route filenames name the demo
targets: **Kesselberg, Tegernsee, Ammersee, Sylvenstein, Fischbachau**.

Own this on stage: *"BMW's crowd data is Bavarian, so we demo where the riders
actually are."* That's a strength, not an apology.

### The narrative beat (verified numbers — these reconcile)

Of userA's 89 planned routes, 74 carry route options. **69 of those 74 (93%) are
set to `optimization="fastest"`, only 5 to `"winding"`; `windingness` is on the
`medium` default in every single one.** Yet his lean-angle traces show a rider
hunting corners.

> The rider told the app he wanted the *fastest* route 93% of the time. His bike
> says otherwise. We don't ask riders what they want — we read it off the
> motorcycle.

---

## The definition of a "good route"

Per ~100 m morton cell `c`, all features **normalised per kilometre** (this is
the fix to BMW's own formula, see below), each scaled to [0,1] by crowd
percentile:

**Fun features**
- `curviness` = Σ|Δlean| / km, ignoring steps < 2° as sensor noise (BMW's own
  definition, `app.js:188`)
- `lean_quality` = share of cell distance ridden beyond ±5° lean
- `sweet_spot` = share of samples in the brief's green-flag band, 50–120 km/h
- `flow` = 1 − share of samples below 20 km/h (the "standstills" red flag)
- `elev_gain` = |Δ mean elevation| per km between adjacent cells
- `rpm_engagement` = mean engine speed, percentile-scaled

**Safety / red-flag features**
- `abs_rate` = ABS activations per km — a crowd-sourced road-surface and
  road-hazard proxy that no competitor has
- `hard_decel_rate` = samples below −3 m/s² per km
- `lean_demand` = crowd p95 |lean| in the cell → used for capability matching
- `urban_penalty` = low mean speed + high speed variance (the "inner city" flag)

**External features**
- `rain`, `temp`, `wind` from Open-Meteo at ride time
- `scenic` = OSM viewpoints / lakes / passes within ~500 m, plus elevation
  variance as a fallback proxy

### Fun score

```
fun(c, rider) = Σ_f  w_f(rider) · feature_f(c)        # w normalised, Σw = 1
risk(c, rider) = w_abs·abs_rate + w_dec·hard_decel + w_cap·capability_gap
                 + w_wx·weather_penalty
```

where `capability_gap = max(0, crowd_p95_lean(c) − rider_p95_lean)` — we do not
send a rider whose own lean envelope tops out at 20° onto a road the crowd only
rides well at 45°. **That single term uses crowd data and personal data together
to produce a safety outcome, which is three rubric metrics in one line.**

### Edge cost — why Dijkstra stays valid

For a cell-to-cell edge with length `L` (km) and crowd-observed median speed `v`:

```
time      = L / v(hour_of_day)          # real observed speed, not a speed limit
cost(e)   = time · ( 1 + α·(1 − fun(e)) + β·risk(e) )
```

Every term is positive, so plain Dijkstra/A* is correct — no negative-weight
trap. `α` is the rider's single **"Chill ↔ Full Send" slider**: sweep it to
produce a Pareto set of three routes, and binary-search it to hit a time budget
("I have 90 minutes to get to Tegernsee"). That is the whiteboard's
"time optimized (20 min ≠ 120 min)" requirement, for free.

### Beat BMW's straw-man, out loud

Their reference `funFactor` (`app.js:203`) multiplies by `pathKm` — so a cell
with more ridden road scores higher *regardless of road quality*. It has an
exposure count riding along inside a quality score. Name that on stage, show the
per-km normalised version next to it on the same heatmap, and use crowd trip
count only as a **confidence weight** (shrink toward the regional mean when a
cell has few trips), never as a fun multiplier. This is exactly the
explainability beat the brief promises bonus points for.

---

## Architecture

```
precompute/  ── offline, one pass over 13 GB ──►  data/cells.parquet (~30 MB)
                                                  data/graph.npz
     │
engine/      ── FastAPI: /route, /loop, /profile, /cells ──►
     │
web/         ── fork of BMW's tripViewer (Leaflet, no build step)
     │
fixtures/    ── frozen weather + OSM + scripted demo routes (offline safety net)
```

### 1. `precompute/` — the scalability story

One streaming pass, **16-way multiprocessing over the 512 shard directories**
(the box has 16 cores). Per cell, accumulate only O(1) running sums: point and
trip counts, path metres, Σ|Δlean|, Σ|lean|, leaned metres, speed-band counts,
Σrpm, ABS/ASC counts, hard-decel counts, elevation min/max/Σ, Σ outside temp,
and **hour-of-day × month visit and median-speed histograms**.

Aggregate at **morton level 18 (~100 m cells)**; because the morton code is a
base-4 quadkey, coarser levels are a *string truncation* — level 16 (~400 m) and
14 (~1.6 km) roll up for free for the zoomed-out heatmap. Encoder and scheme are
already documented at `tripViewer/tripViewer/app.js:225`; reuse it verbatim so
our cells line up with BMW's viewer exactly.

whole answer to "Scalability & Efficiency", and it's the same argument at
national scale.

is blocked at the venue, the stdlib `csv` + `multiprocessing` path is only ~2×
slower and still finishes inside 20 minutes — write the reader so it can switch.

Nodes = morton cells that riders have actually ridden. Edges = observed cell→cell

behaviour attached.

ride, at speeds they actually ride them.** It also removes any dependency on
downloading an OSM extract tonight, which is the single biggest schedule risk.

strictly post-Milestone-3.)

compare each feature's mean to the crowd baseline:

```
z_R(f) = ( μ_R(f) − μ_crowd(f) ) / σ_crowd(f)

```

# BMW Ride Planner — Build & Pitch Plan

## Context

BMW Motorrad's track at the TUM.ai Zurich hackathon ("FIND YOUR THRILL — Route
Challenge") asks for a route planner for motorcyclists where the objective is
the *quality of the ride*, not the trip time. We have BMW's dataset on disk and
pitch **tomorrow morning (~09:00–11:00)** — roughly 16 working hours from now.

The brief (`~/Desktop/BMW/20260912 Hackathon Presentation Zürich Short 2.pdf`,
p.2) states the evaluation metrics verbatim. Everything below is organised
against them:

| # | Rubric metric | Where this plan delivers it |
|---|---------------|------------------------------|
| 1 | Usage of BMW **Crowd Data** | 85,699-trip aggregate → the routing graph itself |
| 2 | Usage of BMW **Personal Rider Data** | Revealed-preference weight fitting per rider |
| 3 | Usage of **External Sources** | Open-Meteo weather + OSM scenic POIs |
| 4 | **Scalability & Efficiency** | Morton-prefix precompute: 13 GB → ~30 MB served |
| 5 | Calculation of **Fun Score** | Normalised per-km feature score, explainable on stage |
| 6 | Consideration of **Rider Safety** | Crowd ABS rate + personal lean-capability matching |

Deliverables they name: the exact definition of "good route", an overview of all
data sources and their weighting, a visual route-planning tool, and a live demo
with an algorithm walk-through ("explainability + live demo score bonus points").

### One concern, stated once

You chose **both** use cases at equal weight. In 16 hours that is only feasible
because the joy-ride loop is built as a thin wrapper over the *same* graph, the
*same* scorer and the *same* Dijkstra as A→B — no second engine. The hard rule:
if Milestone 2 (personalised A→B, explainable) is not green by **00:30**, the
loop gets cut and must not appear on a slide. Do not promise on stage what isn't
running on the laptop.

---

## What the data actually contains (verified, not assumed)

`~/Desktop/BMW/exd_download/datasetHackathon/`

- **`anonymizedDataLake/trips-samples-{1,2}/{00..ff}/*.csv`** — **85,699 trips**,
  13 GB, sharded by morton-code prefix. 42 columns, ~1 Hz sampling, median ~310
  rows (~5 min snippets). This is the crowd corpus.
- **`exampleUser{A,B,C}/recordedTrips/*.csv`** — 101 / 73 / 224 full trips (userA
  up to 17,702 rows ≈ 5 h). Same schema. These are the three personal riders.
- **`exampleUserA/plannedRoutes/*.gpx`** — 89 routes the rider *planned in the
  BMW app*, carrying BMW's own option vocabulary:
  `<cnrd:routeOptions optimization="winding|fastest" windingness hilliness>` and
  `<cnrd:avoidances motorways dirtRoads alreadyUsedRoads .../>`.
- **`tripViewer/tripViewer/{app.js,index.html,style.css}`** — BMW's own Leaflet
  viewer. Read it; it is our frontend base and it hands us three things free:
  the **morton grid/heatmap layer**, the **ride playback with live lean/speed
  gauges**, and a documented `funFactor` we can beat.

### Column reality check — read this before writing any feature

Fill rates measured over 150 lake trips and all of userA/B/C:

| Column | Lake | userA | userB | userC | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sensorsbankingangle` | 100% | 89% | 83% | 100% | **The moat.** Backbone of everything. |
| `positionmapmatchedlat/lon` | 100% | 99% | — | — | Use for map-matched geometry |
| `positionrawelevation` | 100% | 99% | 100% | 100% | **Use this** for elevation |
| `positionmapmatchedelevation` | 46% | 70% | — | — | Too sparse — do not use |
| `ridingvehiclespeed` | 88% | 55% | 70% | 80% | Good; fall back to `positionrawspeed` |
| `ridingabsbraking` | 99% | 88% | 86% | 99% | Safety / road-condition signal |
| `ridingenginespeed` | 97% | 82% | — | — | Feeds fun score |
| `ridingthrottlevalue` | 73% | 64% | — | — | Usable with care |
| `sensorsaccelerationlongitudinal` | 99% | 78% | — | — | Braking proxy |
| `sensorsoutsidetemperature` | 94% | 88% | — | — | Historical weather proxy |
| `sensorsbreakpressurefront/rear` | **0%** | 0% | 0% | 0% | **Dead column — never touch it** |
| `sensorsaccelerationlateral` | 70% | **3%** | **5%** | 73% | Works on crowd, empty for 2 of 3 riders — **cannot be in the personal profile** |
| `trip_id` | 56% | 68% | — | — | Unreliable; **use the filename** as trip id |

Three corrections to the whiteboard notes, all of which a BMW engineer in the
room would catch:

1. **Braking is not in brake pressure.** It has to come from `ridingabsbraking`
   plus `sensorsaccelerationlongitudinal`.
2. **Rider age does not exist in this dataset.** Drop it. "Personal Rider Data"
   is a graded metric — claiming a field we don't have is the one thing that
   reads as fabrication. The profile is derived from riding behaviour only.
3. **Bike model is not in the dataset either.** Infer a coarse class
   (rpm-per-km/h ratio, gear count, lean envelope, tyre pressure) *and* let the
   user confirm it in a UI dropdown. Say "inferred, rider-confirmable" on stage.

### Geography — demo in Bavaria, not Zurich

Crowd data is concentrated at **47.6–48.5 N, 11.0–11.9 E** (Munich and its
southern foothills). userA's personal rides reach 43.6–48.9 N, 4.8–13.4 E (the
Alps, Dolomites, South Tyrol). Their own planned-route filenames name the demo
targets: **Kesselberg, Tegernsee, Ammersee, Sylvenstein, Fischbachau**.

Own this on stage: *"BMW's crowd data is Bavarian, so we demo where the riders
actually are."* That's a strength, not an apology.

### The narrative beat (verified numbers — these reconcile)

Of userA's 89 planned routes, 74 carry route options. **69 of those 74 (93%) are
set to `optimization="fastest"`, only 5 to `"winding"`; `windingness` is on the
`medium` default in every single one.** Yet his lean-angle traces show a rider
hunting corners.

> The rider told the app he wanted the *fastest* route 93% of the time. His bike
> says otherwise. We don't ask riders what they want — we read it off the
> motorcycle.

---

## The definition of a "good route"

Per ~100 m morton cell `c`, all features **normalised per kilometre** (this is
the fix to BMW's own formula, see below), each scaled to [0,1] by crowd
percentile:

**Fun features**
- `curviness` = Σ|Δlean| / km, ignoring steps < 2° as sensor noise (BMW's own
  definition, `app.js:188`)
- `lean_quality` = share of cell distance ridden beyond ±5° lean
- `sweet_spot` = share of samples in the brief's green-flag band, 50–120 km/h
- `flow` = 1 − share of samples below 20 km/h (the "standstills" red flag)
- `elev_gain` = |Δ mean elevation| per km between adjacent cells
- `rpm_engagement` = mean engine speed, percentile-scaled

**Safety / red-flag features**
- `abs_rate` = ABS activations per km — a crowd-sourced road-surface and
  road-hazard proxy that no competitor has
- `hard_decel_rate` = samples below −3 m/s² per km
- `lean_demand` = crowd p95 |lean| in the cell → used for capability matching
- `urban_penalty` = low mean speed + high speed variance (the "inner city" flag)

**External features**
- `rain`, `temp`, `wind` from Open-Meteo at ride time
- `scenic` = OSM viewpoints / lakes / passes within ~500 m, plus elevation
  variance as a fallback proxy

### Fun score

```
fun(c, rider) = Σ_f  w_f(rider) · feature_f(c)        # w normalised, Σw = 1
risk(c, rider) = w_abs·abs_rate + w_dec·hard_decel + w_cap·capability_gap
                 + w_wx·weather_penalty
```

where `capability_gap = max(0, crowd_p95_lean(c) − rider_p95_lean)` — we do not
send a rider whose own lean envelope tops out at 20° onto a road the crowd only
rides well at 45°. **That single term uses crowd data and personal data together
to produce a safety outcome, which is three rubric metrics in one line.**

### Edge cost — why Dijkstra stays valid

For a cell-to-cell edge with length `L` (km) and crowd-observed median speed `v`:

```
time      = L / v(hour_of_day)          # real observed speed, not a speed limit
cost(e)   = time · ( 1 + α·(1 − fun(e)) + β·risk(e) )
```

Every term is positive, so plain Dijkstra/A* is correct — no negative-weight
trap. `α` is the rider's single **"Chill ↔ Full Send" slider**: sweep it to
produce a Pareto set of three routes, and binary-search it to hit a time budget
("I have 90 minutes to get to Tegernsee"). That is the whiteboard's
"time optimized (20 min ≠ 120 min)" requirement, for free.

### Beat BMW's straw-man, out loud

Their reference `funFactor` (`app.js:203`) multiplies by `pathKm` — so a cell
with more ridden road scores higher *regardless of road quality*. It has an
exposure count riding along inside a quality score. Name that on stage, show the
per-km normalised version next to it on the same heatmap, and use crowd trip
count only as a **confidence weight** (shrink toward the regional mean when a
cell has few trips), never as a fun multiplier. This is exactly the
explainability beat the brief promises bonus points for.

---

## Architecture

```
precompute/  ── offline, one pass over 13 GB ──►  data/cells.parquet (~30 MB)
                                                  data/graph.npz
     │
engine/      ── FastAPI: /route, /loop, /profile, /cells ──►
     │
web/         ── fork of BMW's tripViewer (Leaflet, no build step)
     │
fixtures/    ── frozen weather + OSM + scripted demo routes (offline safety net)
```

### 1. `precompute/` — the scalability story

One streaming pass, **16-way multiprocessing over the 512 shard directories**
(the box has 16 cores). Per cell, accumulate only O(1) running sums: point and
trip counts, path metres, Σ|Δlean|, Σ|lean|, leaned metres, speed-band counts,
Σrpm, ABS/ASC counts, hard-decel counts, elevation min/max/Σ, Σ outside temp,
and **hour-of-day × month visit and median-speed histograms**.

Aggregate at **morton level 18 (~100 m cells)**; because the morton code is a
base-4 quadkey, coarser levels are a *string truncation* — level 16 (~400 m) and
14 (~1.6 km) roll up for free for the zoomed-out heatmap. Encoder and scheme are
already documented at `tripViewer/tripViewer/app.js:225`; reuse it verbatim so
our cells line up with BMW's viewer exactly.

Output: `cells.parquet` (a few hundred thousand rows, tens of MB). **13 GB of
telemetry answered by a ~30 MB artefact, served in milliseconds** — that is the
whole answer to "Scalability & Efficiency", and it's the same argument at
national scale.

**Temporal prior at a coarser level.** 85,699 trips × ~310 median rows ≈ 27M
points spread over ~10⁵–10⁶ level-18 cells is only a few dozen points per cell —
split across 24 h × 7 days that is mostly empty, and the crowd-congestion claim
is a headline. So accumulate the temporal histogram at **level 14 (~1.6 km)** in
coarse bands (**weekday/weekend × 3 time bands**) while fun and safety features
stay at level 18. Rollup is string truncation, so this is one extra accumulator
dict in the same pass — do it now, not at 02:00 when the buckets come back null.
Consequently `v(hour)` in the edge cost needs a documented fallback chain:
**cell median → level-14 band median → regional median.**

**Dependencies — checked, and worse than assumed.** This box has Python 3.14.6
via miniforge with **numpy, scipy, pandas, polars and fastapi all absent**.
Python 3.14 is new enough that some wheels may not exist, and a source build at
17:30 is fatal. So:

```bash
conda create -y -n bmw python=3.12 numpy scipy polars pyarrow fastapi uvicorn
```

Python 3.12 is where every wheel definitely exists — take that env, don't fight

stop fighting it.** Plan B must cover the *graph* as well as the reader: stdlib
`csv` + `multiprocessing` for the pass (~2× slower, still under 20 min), and
pure `heapq` + dict-of-lists for Dijkstra — 300k nodes / 1M edges runs well
under a second with nothing installed. Write both so the switch is a flag.

### 2. The routing graph — built from the crowd, not from OSM

Nodes = morton cells that riders have actually ridden. Edges = observed cell→cell
transitions in the crowd trips, with observed median speed and observed lean
behaviour attached.

This is deliberate and it is a pitch point: **we route on roads riders actually
ride, at speeds they actually ride them.** It also removes any dependency on
downloading an OSM extract tonight, which is the single biggest schedule risk.
Store as a scipy CSR matrix + node lookup in `graph.npz` (or dict-of-lists on
the stdlib path); ~300k nodes / ~1M edges routes in well under a second with
`heapq`. Snap origin/destination to the nearest cell that has data. (OSM
enrichment for surface tags is optional and strictly post-Milestone-3.)

**Two filters in the edge builder — not optional, and not deferrable.** A trip
with a GPS dropout emits a single "transition" spanning 2–5 km. Dijkstra will
find those and love them: they look like free shortcuts with a plausible
`time = L/v`, and the Munich→Kesselberg acid test can pass while the route
quietly teleports. BMW's own viewer guards against this at `app.js:176` with
`MAX_GAP_M`.

1. **Drop any transition longer than ~150 m** (1.5× the level-18 cell diagonal).
2. **Require ≥ 2 distinct trips per edge.** This also prunes the
   parallel-road-collapse case — a motorway and its frontage road inside one
   100 m cell — down to transitions riders actually made.

### 3. Personal rider profile — revealed preference, 30 lines

For rider `R`: take the cells `R` actually rode, distance-weight them, and
compare each feature's mean to the crowd baseline:

```
z_R(f) = ( μ_R(f) − μ_crowd(f) ) / σ_crowd(f)
w_R(f) = normalise( clip(z_R(f), 0, ∞) )
```

Also extract, per rider: typical ride duration, preferred time of day and month,
**personal p95 lean envelope** (feeds the safety term), and inferred bike class.
Nothing here is a black box — the weights go straight on a bar chart on stage,
next to the 69-of-74-"fastest" slide.

### 4. Joy-ride loop — same engine, thin wrapper

1. Dijkstra once from the origin → time-to-reach for every cell.
2. Take the ring of cells at ≈ T/2 travel time.
3. Pick top-K candidate turnarounds, **spread across bearings** so the options
   look and feel different on the map.
4. For each: route out with fun-weighted cost, then route back with a reuse
   penalty on already-traversed edges — which is literally BMW's own
   `alreadyUsedRoads="allow|forbid"` option, so we speak their vocabulary.
5. Rank complete loops by fun per hour, return the best 3.

No new search code. One Dijkstra, called four times.

Forking the tripViewer beats scaffolding anything tonight: zero build step, and
the demo speaks BMW's own visual language on their own stage.

- **Left panel** — rider (A/B/C), mode toggle **Destination | Joy ride**,

- **Map** — three candidate routes; the existing morton fun-heat layer

- **"Why this route" card** — the weight breakdown, and per route: fun score,

  weighted" deliverable, rendered live instead of on a slide.
- **Ride preview — the demo hero.** The whiteboard's "view the ride before even

  crowd-**predicted** lean and speed per cell. The judge watches the bike lean
  through corners it hasn't ridden yet. Nothing else in the room will do this,
  and it is mostly code BMW wrote.

contract in the **first 30 minutes**; that is the thing that lets all three work
in parallel without blocking.

| Directory | Owner | Scope |

| `engine/` | Krish | fun/risk scoring, Dijkstra, loop, FastAPI, profile fitting |

# BMW Ride Planner — Build Plan v2

## Context

BMW Motorrad's "FIND YOUR THRILL" route challenge (TUM.ai Zurich). Pitch is
**tomorrow morning**. The dataset is on disk at
`~/Desktop/BMW/exd_download/datasetHackathon/`.

This replaces the earlier plan. The new whiteboard pages changed the product
from "a router that scores fun" into **a rider-development companion with a
dashboard** — and that is a much stronger pitch, because the new headline idea
is only possible with BMW's data.

BMW's graded metrics (from the brief, p.2) and where each is earned:

| Rubric metric | Delivered by |
|---|---|
| Usage of BMW **Crowd Data** | 85,699-trip cell aggregate → *is* the routing graph + area metrics view |
| Usage of BMW **Personal Rider Data** | Per-rider profile, fog map, records, growth targeting |
| Usage of **External Sources** | Open-Meteo weather, OSM water/forest/viewpoints, local sun-position math |
| **Scalability & Efficiency** | DuckDB over Parquet + morton-prefix pruning: 13 GB → ~30 MB served |
| Calculation of **Fun Score** | The KPI scorecard below, normalised per-km, explainable live |
| Consideration of **Rider Safety** | Capability ceiling + crowd ABS rate + weather, as a hard constraint |

---

## The product thesis — lead the pitch with this

From the notes: *"Push riders to a safe limit so he learns while being safe."*

Everyone else in the room will build a router that finds twisty roads. The
differentiator on these pages is that the app **develops the rider**: steeper
lean angles than they've ridden, terrain they haven't explored, weather they
haven't ridden in — each pushed only as far as their own demonstrated
capability plus a safety margin.

That single idea unifies the whole dashboard: the fog map shows what's
unexplored, Learnings shows progression, Records show milestones, and the
Growth KPI is what makes a route *worth riding today* rather than just twisty.
And it is impossible without lean-angle telemetry, which is BMW's moat —
**phones don't measure lean angle**.

> Strava tells you what you did. We tell you what you're ready for.

---

## Data reality — verified, read before building anything

- **Crowd:** `anonymizedDataLake/trips-samples-{1,2}/{00..ff}/*.csv` — **85,699
  trips**, 13 GB, ~1 Hz, sharded by morton prefix, median ~310 rows.
- **Riders:** `exampleUser{A,B,C}/recordedTrips/*.csv` — 101 / 73 / 224 full
  trips. userA's own rides span 43.6–48.9 N, 4.8–13.4 E (Alps, Dolomites).
- **Planned routes:** `exampleUserA/plannedRoutes/*.gpx` — 89 files with BMW's
  option vocabulary (`optimization`, `windingness`, `alreadyUsedRoads`).
- **BMW's viewer:** `tripViewer/tripViewer/app.js` — reuse its morton encoder
  (`:225`), curviness definition (`:188`), gap guard (`:176`), and playback
  gauges. Do not re-derive any of them.

**Column verdicts (measured fill rates):**

| Column | Lake | A / B / C | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sensorsbankingangle` | 100% | 89 / 83 / 100% | **The moat** — lean, curviness, capability, growth |
| `positionrawelevation` | 100% | 99 / 100 / 100% | Altitude KPI. Use this, **not** `positionmapmatchedelevation` (46%) |
| `ridingvehiclespeed` | 88% | 55 / 70 / 80% | Speed KPIs; fall back to `positionrawspeed` |
| `ridingabsbraking` | 99% | 88 / 86 / 99% | Road-condition + safety signal |
| `ridingenginespeed` | 97% | 82% | Engagement; bike-class inference |
| `sensorsoutsidetemperature` | 94% | 88% | "Weather conditions ridden in" (rider history) |
| `sensorsbreakpressurefront/rear` | **0%** | 0% | **Dead column. Never reference it.** |
| `sensorsaccelerationlateral` | 70% | **3 / 5 / 73%** | Crowd-only — **must not enter the personal profile** |
| `trip_id` | 56% | 68% | Unreliable — **use the filename** as trip id |

**Three claims in the notes that the data cannot support — drop them now:**
1. **Rider age** is not in the dataset. Profiles are behavioural only.
2. **Bike model** is not either. Infer a coarse class (rpm-per-km/h, gear count,
   lean envelope, tyre pressure) and let the rider confirm it in the UI.
3. **Road construction** has no live source tonight. Either use OSM
   `highway=construction` from the cached extract or drop the KPI — do not
   pretend it's live.

**Geography:** crowd data is Bavarian (47.6–48.5 N, 11.0–11.9 E). Demo Munich →
**Kesselberg / Tegernsee / Ammersee** — roads that appear in userA's own planned
route filenames. Say on stage: *"BMW's crowd data is Bavarian, so we demo where
the riders are."*

**The narrative slide (numbers reconcile — checked):** of userA's 89 planned
routes, 74 carry options; **69 of those 74 (93%) are set to
`optimization="fastest"` and `windingness` is on the `medium` default in every
single one.** He never told the app he wanted a fun route. His lean traces say
he's a corner-hunter. *We don't ask riders what they want — we read it off the
motorcycle.*

---

## The KPI scorecard

Every KPI is computed per **morton cell at level 18 (~100 m)**, normalised
**per kilometre** and percentile-scaled to [0,1] against the crowd. Time-varying
KPIs are marked **f(t)** and evaluated at the ride's planned start time.

### a) Scenic score — f(t)

| KPI | Source |
|---|---|
| Curviness | Σ|Δlean| per km, 2° noise floor — crowd |
| Road type | Inferred from crowd speed profile + OSM class; penalise motorway & inner city |
| Trees / nature | OSM `landuse=forest`, `natural=wood`, cached |
| Water | OSM `natural=water`, lakes and rivers, cached |
| Altitude | `positionrawelevation` mean + gain per km |
| Max speed allowed | OSM `maxspeed` where present, else crowd p85 speed |
| **Sunset window f(t)** | Sun azimuth/elevation computed locally (NOAA formula, ~20 lines, no API) vs road bearing + open western aspect |
| **Lack of traffic f(t)** | Crowd median speed by weekday/weekend × time band ÷ that cell's free-flow p85 |
| Music | **Cut.** No data, no time. Do not put it on a slide. |

### b) Rider profile — Sportive / Safer / Chill

Three presets seed the weights; the rider's own telemetry then adjusts them.

| KPI | Source |
|---|---|
| Sharp angles | Rider p50 / p90 / p95 |lean| |
| Speed relative to max | Rider speed ÷ crowd p85 in the same cells |
| Type of bike | Inferred class, rider-confirmable in UI |
| Free time for riding | Histogram of their trip start times, weekday × hour, and typical duration |
| Weather conditions history | Distribution of `sensorsoutsidetemperature` across their trips |

**Revealed-preference weight fitting** — transparent, ~30 lines:
```
z_R(f) = ( μ_R(f) − μ_crowd(f) ) / σ_crowd(f)      # distance-weighted over ridden cells
w_R(f) = normalise( clip(z_R(f), 0, ∞) )
```
These weights go straight onto a bar chart in the UI. No black box.

### c) Safety — a constraint, not just a penalty

| KPI | Source |
|---|---|
| Rain / snow | Open-Meteo precipitation at ride time; temp < 8 °C is the brief's red flag |
| Traffic | Crowd temporal prior (above) |
| ABS rate | ABS activations per km — crowd-sourced road-surface proxy nobody else has |
| Hard decel rate | Samples below −3 m/s² per km |
| **Capability ceiling** | `crowd_p95_lean(cell) − rider_p95_lean` |
| Road construction | OSM `highway=construction` if cached, else drop |

`capability_gap > margin` is a **hard exclusion**, not a soft penalty. We do not
route a 20°-lean rider onto a road the crowd only rides well at 45°.

### d) Growth — the differentiator

| KPI | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Lean stretch** | Reward cells whose crowd p50 lean demand sits just **above** the rider's p90 and **below** their p99 — a stretch, never a cliff |
| **New terrain** | Cell's level-14 morton prefix not in the rider's visited set (drives the fog map) |
| **New conditions** | Weather/temperature band the rider has not ridden in, only when safety allows |
| **Records in reach** | Distance to their personal best max-lean / max-altitude / longest-ride |

Growth is always clipped by the safety constraint. That's the "safe limit so he
learns while being safe" line, expressed as arithmetic.

---

## Route generation

One graph, one scorer, two search strategies.

**Graph:** nodes are level-18 cells riders have actually ridden; edges are
observed cell→cell transitions from the crowd, carrying observed median speed.
We route on **roads riders actually ride, at speeds they actually ride them** —
and it needs no OSM download to function.

**Two filters in the edge builder — not deferrable.** A GPS dropout emits one
"transition" spanning kilometres, and Dijkstra will love it: a free shortcut
with a plausible `time = L/v`. BMW guards this at `app.js:176`.
1. Drop transitions longer than **~150 m** (1.5× level-18 cell diagonal).
2. Require **≥ 2 distinct trips per edge** — also prunes parallel-road collapse
   (motorway + frontage road inside one cell).

**Value and cost:**
```
value(e,t) = w_scenic·scenic(e,t) + w_fun·curviness(e) + w_growth·growth(e,R)
risk(e,t)  = w_abs·abs_rate + w_dec·hard_decel + w_wx·weather + w_traffic·congestion
time(e,t)  = L / v(e, time_band)

cost(e,t)  = time(e,t) · ( 1 + α·(1 − value(e,t)) + β·risk(e,t) )
excluded   if capability_gap(e,R) > margin
```
All terms positive → plain Dijkstra is correct, no negative-weight trap.
`v` fallback chain: **cell median → level-14 band median → regional median.**

`α` is the UI's **Chill ↔ Sportive** slider. Sweep it for three route options
(Chill / Balanced / Full Send); binary-search it to hit a time budget — that's
the notes' *"time optimized (20 min ≠ 120 min)"* requirement, for free.

**Mode 1 — Destination (A→B).** Dijkstra on the above. Time budget via `α`
search, ±10% tolerance.

**Mode 2 — Joyride (X hours, return home).** Four calls to the *same* Dijkstra:
1. Dijkstra from origin → time-to-reach for every cell.
2. Take the ring of cells at ≈ T/2.
3. Pick top-K turnarounds, **spread across bearings** so options look different.
4. Route out fun-weighted, return with a **reuse penalty** on traversed edges —
   literally BMW's own `alreadyUsedRoads` option, so we speak their vocabulary.
5. Rank loops by value per hour, return best 3.

**Sunset scheduling** is the joyride showpiece: because scenic is f(t), the
planner can place the west-facing viewpoint leg inside the golden-hour window.
*"Leave at 18:10 and you'll be at the Kesselberg overlook facing west at
sunset."* One formula, unforgettable demo moment.

**Temporal prior must be coarse.** 85,699 × ~310 rows ≈ 27M points over ~10⁵–10⁶
level-18 cells is a few dozen points per cell; split by 24 h × 7 d it is mostly
empty. Accumulate the temporal histogram at **level 14 (~1.6 km)** in
**weekday/weekend × 3 time bands**, while fun/safety stay at level 18. Morton
rollup is string truncation, so this is one extra `GROUP BY` in the same pass.

---

## Tech stack

Everything below is **verified installable on this box right now** — `duckdb`,
`fastapi`, `uvicorn`, `numpy`, `pyarrow` all have cp314 wheels for the installed
Python 3.14.6, and Node v20.20.2 / npm 10.8.2 are present. No conda env needed.

| Layer | Choice | Why this one |
|---|---|---|
| Precompute | **DuckDB + Parquet** | The whole cell aggregation is *one SQL query*. `lag(sensorsbankingangle) OVER (PARTITION BY trip ORDER BY timestampinmillis)` gives Σ|Δlean| directly; `read_csv` globs all 85,699 files; it spills to disk (only ~6 GB RAM free). Hundreds of lines of multiprocessing replaced by one query — and columnar + morton-prefix pruning *is* the scalability slide. |
| API | **FastAPI + uvicorn** | Async, auto OpenAPI docs (free "algorithm walk-through" artefact), reads Parquet through DuckDB per request |
| Routing | **Python `heapq` Dijkstra** over a Parquet edge list | 300k nodes / 1M edges routes in well under a second. No scipy dependency needed. |
| Frontend | **Vite + React (JSX, not TS) + Leaflet + Tailwind + Recharts** | See revision note below |
| Map | **Leaflet**, tiles **pre-cached locally** | Same library BMW's own viewer uses; the morton grid/heat layer ports straight over |
| Weather | **Open-Meteo** | No API key, hourly precip/temp/wind, cached to disk with a frozen fallback |
| Geo POIs | **Overpass**, fetched once → `fixtures/` | Water, forest, viewpoints, maxspeed. **Never called live during the demo.** |
| Sun position | **Local NOAA formula** | ~20 lines, zero dependencies, powers the sunset KPI |
| Trip emotions / tags | **Local JSON file** | Emoji tagging needs persistence, not a database |
| Traffic | **No API.** Crowd temporal prior | No free keyless real-time source exists. Deriving congestion from BMW's own 85,699 trips is *stronger* than a stubbed API and scores another crowd-data point. Say exactly that on stage. |

### Revision note: React instead of vanilla JS

Earlier the answer was "Python + plain JS/Leaflet". These pages changed that —
the notes now specify **seven dashboard views** with cards, charts, tabs, a fog
map and a stats page. Vanilla JS state management across seven views is where
the night gets eaten; `npm create vite` costs two minutes. Recharts also gives
the Learnings progression charts essentially free.

Keep JSX, not TypeScript — types are friction at 02:00 with no payoff by 09:00.
If React isn't comfortable for all three of you, say so and the plan reverts to
a tabbed vanilla build with the dashboard trimmed to three views.

### Repo layout — one owner per directory

```
precompute/    DuckDB SQL + runner → data/cells.parquet, data/edges.parquet
engine/        FastAPI: scoring, Dijkstra, joyride, profile fitting, suggestions
web/           Vite + React dashboard
fixtures/      frozen weather / OSM / demo routes / map tiles
data/          generated artefacts (gitignored)
```

| Directory | Owner |
|---|---|
| `precompute/` | one owner |
| `engine/` | Krish |
| `web/` | one owner |

topology, is what stops three people blocking each other. Commit straight to
`dev`; `main` only via PR, and Krish merges.

---

## Connecting the dataset to the viewer

The unification that makes the whole thing cheap: **one `Track` shape serves
both a recorded ride and a planned route.**

```json
{ "id": "...", "kind": "recorded" | "planned",
  "points": [ { "lat":…, "lon":…, "elev":…, "t":…,
                "speed":…, "lean":…, "rpm":…, "abs":… } ],
  "kpis":   { "fun":…, "scenic":…, "safety":…, "growth":…,
              "km":…, "minutes":…, "curviness":…, "elev_gain":… },
  "stops":  [ { "lat":…, "lon":…, "type":"viewpoint|water|coffee", "name":… } ] }
```

- **Recorded** → `GET /trips/{id}/track` reads that trip's CSV through DuckDB.
  Real telemetry, real gauges.
- **Planned** → `GET /route` returns the same shape, with `speed` and `lean`

judge watches the bike lean through corners it hasn't ridden yet. That is the

### API surface

```
GET  /riders                        A, B, C (+ any imported)
GET  /riders/{id}/profile           weights, lean envelope, bike class, free-time histogram
GET  /riders/{id}/trips             list + per-trip KPIs
GET  /riders/{id}/coverage          visited level-14 cells → fog map
GET  /riders/{id}/learnings         progression series + records + next challenge
GET  /riders/{id}/suggestions       Airbnb-style cards
POST /riders/import                 point at a folder of recordedTrips
GET  /cells?bbox=&level=&metric=    crowd area metrics layer
```

telemetry.

The crowd layer, per morton cell, switchable metric (curviness / lean / speed /

the data and algorithm"* deliverable, and it's also our own debugging tool.

# BMW Ride Planner — Build Plan v2

## Context

BMW Motorrad's "FIND YOUR THRILL" route challenge (TUM.ai Zurich). Pitch is
**tomorrow morning**. The dataset is on disk at
`~/Desktop/BMW/exd_download/datasetHackathon/`.

This replaces the earlier plan. The new whiteboard pages changed the product
from "a router that scores fun" into **a rider-development companion with a
dashboard** — and that is a much stronger pitch, because the new headline idea
is only possible with BMW's data.

BMW's graded metrics (from the brief, p.2) and where each is earned:

| Rubric metric | Delivered by |
|---|---|
| Usage of BMW **Crowd Data** | 85,699-trip cell aggregate → *is* the routing graph + area metrics view |
| Usage of BMW **Personal Rider Data** | Per-rider profile, fog map, records, growth targeting |
| Usage of **External Sources** | Open-Meteo weather, OSM water/forest/viewpoints, local sun-position math |
| **Scalability & Efficiency** | DuckDB over Parquet + morton-prefix pruning: 13 GB → ~30 MB served |
| Calculation of **Fun Score** | The KPI scorecard below, normalised per-km, explainable live |
| Consideration of **Rider Safety** | Capability ceiling + crowd ABS rate + weather, as a hard constraint |

---

## The product thesis — lead the pitch with this

From the notes: *"Push riders to a safe limit so he learns while being safe."*

Everyone else in the room will build a router that finds twisty roads. The
differentiator on these pages is that the app **develops the rider**: steeper
lean angles than they've ridden, terrain they haven't explored, weather they
haven't ridden in — each pushed only as far as their own demonstrated
capability plus a safety margin.

That single idea unifies the whole dashboard: the fog map shows what's
unexplored, Learnings shows progression, Records show milestones, and the
Growth KPI is what makes a route *worth riding today* rather than just twisty.
And it is impossible without lean-angle telemetry, which is BMW's moat —
**phones don't measure lean angle**.

> Strava tells you what you did. We tell you what you're ready for.

---

## Data reality — verified, read before building anything

- **Crowd:** `anonymizedDataLake/trips-samples-{1,2}/{00..ff}/*.csv` — **85,699
  trips**, 13 GB, ~1 Hz, sharded by morton prefix, median ~310 rows.
- **Riders:** `exampleUser{A,B,C}/recordedTrips/*.csv` — 101 / 73 / 224 full
  trips. userA's own rides span 43.6–48.9 N, 4.8–13.4 E (Alps, Dolomites).
- **Planned routes:** `exampleUserA/plannedRoutes/*.gpx` — 89 files with BMW's
  option vocabulary (`optimization`, `windingness`, `alreadyUsedRoads`).
- **BMW's viewer:** `tripViewer/tripViewer/app.js` — reuse its morton encoder
  (`:225`), curviness definition (`:188`), gap guard (`:176`), and playback
  gauges. Do not re-derive any of them.

**Column verdicts (measured fill rates):**

| Column | Lake | A / B / C | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sensorsbankingangle` | 100% | 89 / 83 / 100% | **The moat** — lean, curviness, capability, growth |
| `positionrawelevation` | 100% | 99 / 100 / 100% | Altitude KPI. Use this, **not** `positionmapmatchedelevation` (46%) |
| `ridingvehiclespeed` | 88% | 55 / 70 / 80% | Speed KPIs; fall back to `positionrawspeed` |
| `ridingabsbraking` | 99% | 88 / 86 / 99% | Road-condition + safety signal |
| `ridingenginespeed` | 97% | 82% | Engagement; bike-class inference |
| `sensorsoutsidetemperature` | 94% | 88% | "Weather conditions ridden in" (rider history) |
| `sensorsbreakpressurefront/rear` | **0%** | 0% | **Dead column. Never reference it.** |
| `sensorsaccelerationlateral` | 70% | **3 / 5 / 73%** | Crowd-only — **must not enter the personal profile** |
| `trip_id` | 56% | 68% | Unreliable — **use the filename** as trip id |

**Three claims in the notes that the data cannot support — drop them now:**
1. **Rider age** is not in the dataset. Profiles are behavioural only.
2. **Bike model** is not either. Infer a coarse class (rpm-per-km/h, gear count,
   lean envelope, tyre pressure) and let the rider confirm it in the UI.
3. **Road construction** has no live source tonight. Either use OSM
   `highway=construction` from the cached extract or drop the KPI — do not
   pretend it's live.

**Geography:** crowd data is Bavarian (47.6–48.5 N, 11.0–11.9 E). Demo Munich →
**Kesselberg / Tegernsee / Ammersee** — roads that appear in userA's own planned
route filenames. Say on stage: *"BMW's crowd data is Bavarian, so we demo where
the riders are."*

**The narrative slide (numbers reconcile — checked):** of userA's 89 planned
routes, 74 carry options; **69 of those 74 (93%) are set to
`optimization="fastest"` and `windingness` is on the `medium` default in every
single one.** He never told the app he wanted a fun route. His lean traces say
he's a corner-hunter. *We don't ask riders what they want — we read it off the
motorcycle.*

---

## The KPI scorecard

Every KPI is computed per **morton cell at level 18 (~100 m)**, normalised
**per kilometre** and percentile-scaled to [0,1] against the crowd. Time-varying
KPIs are marked **f(t)** and evaluated at the ride's planned start time.

### a) Scenic score — f(t)

| KPI | Source |
|---|---|
| Curviness | Σ|Δlean| per km, 2° noise floor — crowd |
| Road type | Inferred from crowd speed profile + OSM class; penalise motorway & inner city |
| Trees / nature | OSM `landuse=forest`, `natural=wood`, cached |
| Water | OSM `natural=water`, lakes and rivers, cached |
| Altitude | `positionrawelevation` mean + gain per km |
| Max speed allowed | OSM `maxspeed` where present, else crowd p85 speed |
| **Sunset window f(t)** | Sun azimuth/elevation computed locally (NOAA formula, ~20 lines, no API) vs road bearing + open western aspect |
| **Lack of traffic f(t)** | Crowd median speed by weekday/weekend × time band ÷ that cell's free-flow p85 |
| Music | **Cut.** No data, no time. Do not put it on a slide. |

### b) Rider profile — Sportive / Safer / Chill

Three presets seed the weights; the rider's own telemetry then adjusts them.

| KPI | Source |
|---|---|
| Sharp angles | Rider p50 / p90 / p95 |lean| |
| Speed relative to max | Rider speed ÷ crowd p85 in the same cells |
| Type of bike | Inferred class, rider-confirmable in UI |
| Free time for riding | Histogram of their trip start times, weekday × hour, and typical duration |
| Weather conditions history | Distribution of `sensorsoutsidetemperature` across their trips |

**Revealed-preference weight fitting** — transparent, ~30 lines:
```
z_R(f) = ( μ_R(f) − μ_crowd(f) ) / σ_crowd(f)      # distance-weighted over ridden cells
w_R(f) = normalise( clip(z_R(f), 0, ∞) )
```
These weights go straight onto a bar chart in the UI. No black box.

### c) Safety — a constraint, not just a penalty

| KPI | Source |
|---|---|
| Rain / snow | Open-Meteo precipitation at ride time; temp < 8 °C is the brief's red flag |
| Traffic | Crowd temporal prior (above) |
| ABS rate | ABS activations per km — crowd-sourced road-surface proxy nobody else has |
| Hard decel rate | Samples below −3 m/s² per km |
| **Capability ceiling** | `crowd_p95_lean(cell) − rider_p95_lean` |
| Road construction | OSM `highway=construction` if cached, else drop |

`capability_gap > margin` is a **hard exclusion**, not a soft penalty. We do not
route a 20°-lean rider onto a road the crowd only rides well at 45°.

### d) Growth — the differentiator

| KPI | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Lean stretch** | Reward cells whose crowd p50 lean demand sits just **above** the rider's p90 and **below** their p99 — a stretch, never a cliff |
| **New terrain** | Cell's level-14 morton prefix not in the rider's visited set (drives the fog map) |
| **New conditions** | Weather/temperature band the rider has not ridden in, only when safety allows |
| **Records in reach** | Distance to their personal best max-lean / max-altitude / longest-ride |

Growth is always clipped by the safety constraint. That's the "safe limit so he
learns while being safe" line, expressed as arithmetic.

---

## Route generation

One graph, one scorer, two search strategies.

**Graph:** nodes are level-18 cells riders have actually ridden; edges are
observed cell→cell transitions from the crowd, carrying observed median speed.
We route on **roads riders actually ride, at speeds they actually ride them** —
and it needs no OSM download to function.

**Two filters in the edge builder — not deferrable.** A GPS dropout emits one
"transition" spanning kilometres, and Dijkstra will love it: a free shortcut
with a plausible `time = L/v`. BMW guards this at `app.js:176`.
1. Drop transitions longer than **~150 m** (1.5× level-18 cell diagonal).
2. Require **≥ 2 distinct trips per edge** — also prunes parallel-road collapse
   (motorway + frontage road inside one cell).

**Value and cost:**
```
value(e,t) = w_scenic·scenic(e,t) + w_fun·curviness(e) + w_growth·growth(e,R)
risk(e,t)  = w_abs·abs_rate + w_dec·hard_decel + w_wx·weather + w_traffic·congestion
time(e,t)  = L / v(e, time_band)

cost(e,t)  = time(e,t) · ( 1 + α·(1 − value(e,t)) + β·risk(e,t) )
excluded   if capability_gap(e,R) > margin
```
All terms positive → plain Dijkstra is correct, no negative-weight trap.
`v` fallback chain: **cell median → level-14 band median → regional median.**

`α` is the UI's **Chill ↔ Sportive** slider. Sweep it for three route options
(Chill / Balanced / Full Send); binary-search it to hit a time budget — that's
the notes' *"time optimized (20 min ≠ 120 min)"* requirement, for free.

**Mode 1 — Destination (A→B).** Dijkstra on the above. Time budget via `α`
search, ±10% tolerance.

**Mode 2 — Joyride (X hours, return home).** Four calls to the *same* Dijkstra:
1. Dijkstra from origin → time-to-reach for every cell.
2. Take the ring of cells at ≈ T/2.
3. Pick top-K turnarounds, **spread across bearings** so options look different.
4. Route out fun-weighted, return with a **reuse penalty** on traversed edges —
   literally BMW's own `alreadyUsedRoads` option, so we speak their vocabulary.
5. Rank loops by value per hour, return best 3.

**Sunset scheduling** is the joyride showpiece: because scenic is f(t), the
planner can place the west-facing viewpoint leg inside the golden-hour window.
*"Leave at 18:10 and you'll be at the Kesselberg overlook facing west at
sunset."* One formula, unforgettable demo moment.

**Temporal prior must be coarse.** 85,699 × ~310 rows ≈ 27M points over ~10⁵–10⁶
level-18 cells is a few dozen points per cell; split by 24 h × 7 d it is mostly
empty. Accumulate the temporal histogram at **level 14 (~1.6 km)** in
**weekday/weekend × 3 time bands**, while fun/safety stay at level 18. Morton
rollup is string truncation, so this is one extra `GROUP BY` in the same pass.

---

## Tech stack

Everything below is **verified installable on this box right now** — `duckdb`,
`fastapi`, `uvicorn`, `numpy`, `pyarrow` all have cp314 wheels for the installed
Python 3.14.6, and Node v20.20.2 / npm 10.8.2 are present. No conda env needed.

| Layer | Choice | Why this one |
|---|---|---|
| Precompute | **DuckDB + Parquet** | The whole cell aggregation is *one SQL query*: `read_csv('…/**/*.csv', filename=true)` globs all 85,699 files, and `lag(sensorsbankingangle) OVER (PARTITION BY filename ORDER BY timestampinmillis)` gives Σ|Δlean| directly. It spills to disk (only ~6 GB RAM free). Hundreds of lines of multiprocessing replaced by one query — and columnar + morton-prefix pruning *is* the scalability slide. |

> **Partition by `filename`, never by `trip_id`.** `trip_id` is only 56% filled
> in the lake — partitioning on it merges ~44% of rows into one null partition
> and silently corrupts every Δlean across trip boundaries. This is in the
> critical path before the 13 GB run; get it right the first time.
| API | **FastAPI + uvicorn** | Async, auto OpenAPI docs (free "algorithm walk-through" artefact), reads Parquet through DuckDB per request |
| Routing | **Python `heapq` Dijkstra** over a Parquet edge list | 300k nodes / 1M edges routes in well under a second. No scipy dependency needed. |
| Frontend | **Vite + React (JSX, not TS) + Leaflet + Tailwind + Recharts** | See revision note below |
| Map | **Leaflet**, tiles **pre-cached locally** | Same library BMW's own viewer uses; the morton grid/heat layer ports straight over |
| Weather | **Open-Meteo** | No API key, hourly precip/temp/wind, cached to disk with a frozen fallback |
| Geo POIs | **Overpass**, fetched once → `fixtures/` | Water, forest, viewpoints, maxspeed. **Never called live during the demo.** |
| Sun position | **Local NOAA formula** | ~20 lines, zero dependencies, powers the sunset KPI |
| Trip emotions / tags | **Local JSON file** | Emoji tagging needs persistence, not a database |
| Traffic | **No API.** Crowd temporal prior | No free keyless real-time source exists. Deriving congestion from BMW's own 85,699 trips is *stronger* than a stubbed API and scores another crowd-data point. Say exactly that on stage. |

### Revision note: React instead of vanilla JS

Earlier the answer was "Python + plain JS/Leaflet". These pages changed that —
the notes now specify **seven dashboard views** with cards, charts, tabs, a fog
map and a stats page. Vanilla JS state management across seven views is where
the night gets eaten; `npm create vite` costs two minutes. Recharts also gives
the Learnings progression charts essentially free.

Keep JSX, not TypeScript — types are friction at 02:00 with no payoff by 09:00.
If React isn't comfortable for all three of you, say so and the plan reverts to
a tabbed vanilla build with the dashboard trimmed to three views.

### Repo layout — one owner per directory

```
precompute/    DuckDB SQL + runner → data/cells.parquet, data/edges.parquet
engine/        FastAPI: scoring, Dijkstra, joyride, profile fitting, suggestions
web/           Vite + React dashboard
fixtures/      frozen weather / OSM / demo routes / map tiles
data/          generated artefacts (gitignored)
```

| Directory | Owner |
|---|---|
| `precompute/` | one owner |
| `engine/` | Krish |
| `web/` | one owner |

topology, is what stops three people blocking each other. Commit straight to
`dev`; `main` only via PR, and Krish merges.

---

## Connecting the dataset to the viewer

The unification that makes the whole thing cheap: **one `Track` shape serves
both a recorded ride and a planned route.**

```json
{ "id": "...", "kind": "recorded" | "planned",
  "points": [ { "lat":…, "lon":…, "elev":…, "t":…,
                "speed":…, "lean":…, "rpm":…, "abs":… } ],
  "kpis":   { "fun":…, "scenic":…, "safety":…, "growth":…,
              "km":…, "minutes":…, "curviness":…, "elev_gain":… },
  "stops":  [ { "lat":…, "lon":…, "type":"viewpoint|water|coffee", "name":… } ] }
```

- **Recorded** → `GET /trips/{id}/track` reads that trip's CSV through DuckDB.
  Real telemetry, real gauges.
- **Planned** → `GET /route` returns the same shape, with `speed` and `lean`
  filled from **crowd-predicted per-cell values** along the chosen path.

One renderer, one playback component, one set of gauges — so **"view the ride
before you even go on it"** (from the first set of notes) is nearly free. The
judge watches the bike lean through corners it hasn't ridden yet. That is the
demo hero, and most of the code is BMW's own.

### API surface

```
GET  /riders                        A, B, C (+ any imported)
GET  /riders/{id}/profile           weights, lean envelope, bike class, free-time histogram
GET  /riders/{id}/trips             list + per-trip KPIs
GET  /riders/{id}/coverage          visited level-14 cells → fog map
GET  /riders/{id}/learnings         progression series + records + next challenge
GET  /riders/{id}/suggestions       Airbnb-style cards
POST /riders/import                 point at a folder of recordedTrips
GET  /cells?bbox=&level=&metric=    crowd area metrics layer
GET  /trips/{id}/track              recorded Track
POST /route                         {rider, from, to, start_time, alpha, budget} → 3 Tracks
POST /joyride                       {rider, origin, hours, start_time, alpha}   → 3 Tracks
POST /trips/{id}/tag                emoji / emotion
```

---

## UI / UX

Single-page dashboard. **Rider switcher pinned in the header** (A / B / C +
"Import rider" → `POST /riders/import`); every view reacts to it, so switching
rider mid-demo re-profiles the whole dashboard live. That's a strong on-stage
moment: same road, three riders, three different scores and three different
routes.

Left nav, seven views:

**1. Overview** *(the "Greeting")*
"Good evening, Rider A." Weather now + ride-window forecast. **Detected free
time** from their own history ("you usually ride Saturday 09:00–13:00 — next
window is dry and 19 °C"). One hero suggestion card. Latest records.

**2. Plan** *(the core)*
Mode toggle **Destination | Joyride** · profile chips **Sportive / Safer /
Chill** · time budget · **start time** (drives every f(t) KPI) · bike confirm.
Map with three route options; crowd fun-heat underneath; scenic stops pinned.
Per route: the KPI breakdown bars, and a **"Why this route"** card naming the
weights and the data behind each. **Ride Preview** plays the route with
predicted lean/speed gauges.

**3. Suggestions** — Airbnb-style cards
Mini-map thumbnail, title, scenic score, duration, and badges: `New terrain` ·
`Sunset window` · `Revisit` · `Stretch your lean`. Cards come from
`/riders/{id}/suggestions`; clicking one loads it into **Plan**.

**4. Past trips**
List + map. Per trip: metrics, riding style, records set, and **emoji emotion
tagging** (persisted to JSON). Any trip loads into the viewer with real
telemetry.

**5. Explore — fog map**
Fog-of-war over level-14 morton cells the rider has visited. "You've explored
18% of Bavaria." Unexplored *fun-dense* areas glow as targets — this is where
the New-terrain growth KPI becomes visible, and it's the most screenshot-able
view in the app.

**6. Learnings**
Progression over time: max lean, terrains explored, weather conditions ridden,
altitude reached. Records wall. **"Your next challenge"** — a concrete road
whose lean demand sits just above their p90, with the safety reasoning shown.

**7. Area metrics**
The crowd layer, per morton cell, switchable metric (curviness / lean / speed /
ABS rate / traffic by time band). This is the brief's *"visual representation of
the data and algorithm"* deliverable, and it's also our own debugging tool.

### Scope tiers — decide with these, not by feel

- **Demo-critical:** Overview, Plan (both modes), Ride Preview, Area metrics,
  rider switching, offline hardening.
- **Should-have:** Suggestions cards, Fog map, Learnings.
- **Cut first, without apology:** emoji tagging, records wall, notifications,

If it isn't running on the laptop by the freeze, it does not go on a slide.

Venue wifi is the most common way a live demo dies.

**Gate 0 — the morton encoder, before any aggregation.** A wrong encoder
invalidates the entire 13 GB pass, and there is exact ground truth: every raw
CSV carries a `morton_code` column. Take 1,000 rows, encode `(lat, lon)` with
the port of `app.js:225`, assert the first 18 base-4 digits equal the row's
`morton_code` prefix. Instant, exact. *(Don't try to load `cells.parquet` into
BMW's tripViewer to check this — it expects the 42-column trip schema.)*

**Precompute** — one shard before all 512:
```bash
python -m precompute.aggregate --shards trips-samples-1/00 --out data/cells_smoke.parquet
```

(passes); no cell with `path_m` ≤ 50 survives; the level-14 temporal buckets are
mostly **non-empty** (if they're null, the level choice was wrong).

trips; then render the longest 20 edges and *look at them*. A teleport that
survives into the demo is worse than a missing feature.

Kesselberg pass; at `α = 0` it must take the A95 motorway. If that inversion
doesn't happen, the cost function is wrong. Time-budget search within ±10%.
(Duration vs `α` steps rather than curves — paths are discrete — so treat
monotonicity as a smoke test only.)

**Safety constraint** — construct a rider with an artificially low lean envelope
and assert the Kesselberg cells are *excluded*, not merely penalised.

**Profiles must differ** — fit A, B and C and confirm three different weight
vectors. userA (Alpine, long tours) and userB (shorter rides, 5% lateral accel)
must not come out identical; if they do, the z-scoring is broken.

# BMW Ride Planner — Plan

Planning docs for the BMW Motorrad track ("FIND YOUR THRILL — Route Challenge")
at the TUM.ai Zurich hackathon. Pitch is the morning of **2026-09-13**.

Read these in order. Each owner needs `01-dataset.md` regardless of which
directory they own.

| Doc | What's in it |
|---|---|
| [01-dataset.md](01-dataset.md) | What the BMW dataset actually contains — measured column fill rates, dead columns, geography, and the three claims in our notes the data cannot support |
| [02-kpis.md](02-kpis.md) | The KPI scorecard (scenic / profile / safety / growth) and the route-generation maths for both ride modes |
| [03-stack.md](03-stack.md) | Tech stack, repo layout, API surface, and how dataset trips and generated routes both load into the viewer |
| [04-ui.md](04-ui.md) | The dashboard — seven views, rider switching, scope tiers |
| [05-execution.md](05-execution.md) | Ownership, hour-by-hour schedule, demo hardening, verification gates |

## The thesis — what we lead the pitch with

From the whiteboard: *"Push riders to a safe limit so he learns while being
safe."*

Everyone else will build a router that finds twisty roads. Ours **develops the
rider** — steeper lean angles than they have ridden, terrain they have not
explored, weather they have not ridden in, each clipped by their own
demonstrated capability plus a safety margin.

That one idea unifies the whole dashboard: the fog map shows what is unexplored,
Learnings shows progression, Records show milestones, and the Growth KPI is what
makes a road worth riding *today* rather than just twisty. It is impossible
without lean-angle telemetry, which is BMW's moat — **phones don't measure lean
angle**.

> Strava tells you what you did. We tell you what you're ready for.

## The narrative slide

Of rider A's 89 planned routes, 74 carry route options. **69 of those 74 (93%)
are set to `optimization="fastest"`, and `windingness` sits on the `medium`
default in every single one.** Yet his lean traces show a rider hunting corners.

> We don't ask riders what they want — we read it off the motorcycle.

## How this maps to BMW's grading

The brief names its evaluation metrics explicitly. Each one is earned here:

| Rubric metric | Delivered by |
|---|---|
| Usage of BMW **Crowd Data** | 85,699-trip cell aggregate → *is* the routing graph, plus the area-metrics view |
| Usage of BMW **Personal Rider Data** | Per-rider profile, fog map, records, growth targeting |
| Usage of **External Sources** | Open-Meteo weather, OSM water/forest/viewpoints, local sun-position maths |
| **Scalability & Efficiency** | DuckDB over Parquet + morton-prefix pruning: 13 GB → ~30 MB served |
| Calculation of **Fun Score** | The KPI scorecard, normalised per-km, explainable live on screen |
| Consideration of **Rider Safety** | Capability ceiling as a hard constraint, plus crowd ABS rate and weather |

Deliverables they ask for: the exact definition of "good route", an overview of
all data sources and their weighting, a visual route-planning tool, and a live
demo with an algorithm walk-through — *"explainability + live demo will score
bonus points."*

Here's the whole thing in plain terms.

## The core trick

Normal routing asks "which way is fastest?" and adds up minutes. We keep using the same search algorithm, but we **lie to it about how long each road takes** — in a controlled, explainable way. A boring road gets told "you're longer than you look." A great road gets told "you're shorter than you look." Then we just ask for the shortest path, and it comes back with a good ride.

That's it. Everything else is deciding *how much* to lie, and being able to show our work.

## Step 1 — Chop the map into squares

We cut Bavaria into ~100 m squares. BMW's dataset already does this: every row has a `morton_code`, which is basically a postcode for a square on the map. Squares that sit next to each other have codes that start with the same digits, so "find everything near here" is a text prefix match — very fast, and it's why this scales.

## Step 2 — Ask 85,699 real rides what each square is like

For every square, we look at every BMW rider who has ever ridden through it and compute:

- **How much did the bike lean?** — and more importantly, how much did the lean *change*. A long steady curve holds one lean angle; a proper set of corners swings left-right-left. Lean change per kilometre is our curviness measure.
- **How fast did people actually go?** — real observed speed, not the speed limit. Also split by time of day, which gives us traffic for free: if a square averages 25 km/h at 08:00 and 70 km/h at 11:00, that's rush hour, measured rather than guessed.
- **Did ABS trigger?** — riders don't trigger ABS on good tarmac. ABS activations per kilometre is a crowd-sourced road-surface and hazard warning that no competitor has.
- **Elevation, temperature, engine revs, hard braking.**

This runs once, offline, over 13 GB. The output is a small table — one row per square, a few tens of megabytes. That reduction is the answer to BMW's "scalability" criterion.

## Step 3 — Build the road network out of the riders themselves

Instead of downloading a map, we say: square X connects to square Y **if riders actually rode from X to Y**. So the network is made of real roads that real motorcyclists actually use, at speeds they actually ride.

One trap here: if someone's GPS drops out for 30 seconds, the data shows a single "hop" spanning three kilometres. The search would adore that — it looks like a free shortcut. So we throw away any hop longer than ~150 m, and require at least two different riders to have made a connection before we trust it.

## Step 4 — Score each square from 0 to 1

Four scores per square, built from your KPI notes:

- **Scenic** — curviness, altitude, forest and water nearby, not a motorway, not inner city, and *sunset timing* (we compute where the sun is and whether the road faces it)
- **Fun** — lean change per km, time spent in the 50–120 km/h band the brief calls a green flag, and "flow" (no standstills)
- **Risk** — rain, cold, ABS rate, hard braking, traffic at that hour
- **Growth** — is this road a bit harder than what you've already ridden? Is it terrain you've never been to?

## Step 5 — Work out what *you* like, from your own bike

We take the squares you've actually ridden and compare them to the average rider. Whatever you over-index on becomes a heavier weight. If your rides are consistently curvier and higher up than the norm, curviness and altitude get pushed up in *your* scoring.

We also measure your **lean envelope** — your personal 95th-percentile lean angle. That does two jobs: it's the safety ceiling, and it's how we find "stretch" roads. A road where the crowd's typical lean is just above your p90 but below your p99 is a road that will teach you something. A road needing 45° when you top out at 20° is excluded outright — not penalised, excluded.

## Step 6 — Turn scores into a cost

For each hop between squares:

```
cost = time × ( 1 + α × (1 − good)  +  β × risk )
```

- `time` is real: hop length ÷ observed speed
- `good` is your personalised blend of scenic + fun + growth
- `α` is the **Chill ↔ Sportive slider** — how much detour you'll accept for a better ride
- Everything stays positive, which is what lets us use standard Dijkstra safely

**A worked example.** Munich → Kesselberg, one 100 m hop on each option:

| | Motorway (A95) | Kesselberg pass |
|---|---|---|
| Observed speed | 120 km/h | 50 km/h |
| Real time | 3.0 s | 7.2 s |
| `good` | 0.1 | 0.9 |
| `risk` | 0.05 | 0.20 |

At `α = 0` (pure speed): motorway 3.0 vs pass 7.2 → **motorway wins**.

At `α = 3` (sportive): motorway `3.0 × (1 + 2.7 + 0.05) = 11.3` vs pass `7.2 × (1 + 0.3 + 0.2) = 10.8` → **the pass wins**, by a little.

Same algorithm, same data, one slider. That inversion is also our main correctness test — if it doesn't flip, the cost function is wrong.

## Step 7 — Search

Dijkstra: spread outward from the start, always expanding the cheapest option so far, until you reach the destination. Under a second on ~300k squares.

**For a destination ride**, that's the whole job. If you say "I have 90 minutes," we run it a handful of times with different `α` and keep the one that lands closest to your budget.

**For a joyride** ("2 hours from here, bring me home"), same search, four calls:
1. Flood outward from home → now we know travel time to every square
2. Take the ring of squares about an hour away
3. Pick a few in different compass directions, so the options actually look different
4. Route out on the fun-weighted cost, then route back with a penalty on roads already used — which is literally BMW's own `alreadyUsedRoads` option, so we're speaking their vocabulary

Because scenic is time-dependent, the planner can also *place* the west-facing leg inside the golden hour: "leave at 18:10 and you'll be at the overlook facing west at sunset."

## How it shows its reasoning

This is where bonus points are, per the brief. Five things on screen:

1. **Your profile, as a bar chart** — "we think you like curves and altitude, because across your 101 rides you ride 1.8× curvier roads than the average BMW rider." Sourced, not asserted.
2. **Per-route KPI bars** — fun, scenic, safety, growth, plus km, minutes, curviness, elevation gain, % of time in the 50–120 band.
3. **The map coloured by *why*** — each stretch tinted by whichever KPI earned it. You can see at a glance "this bit is here for the corners, this bit for the lake, this bit is just the connection out of town."
4. **The road-not-taken panel** — show the fast route beside the chosen one and break down the difference: *"14 minutes slower, 3.2× the lean changes, 340 m more climb, one fewer inner-city crossing."* That's the sentence that wins the room, because it's a trade-off stated honestly rather than a score asserted.
5. **The ride preview** — play the route before riding it, with the lean-angle and speed gauges moving to *predicted* values from crowd data. BMW's own viewer already has that playback component; we just feed it a planned route instead of a recorded one.

And one more that matters for credibility: where we have no crowd data, the UI says so rather than scoring it zero and quietly routing you around a perfectly good road.

## One thing worth being upfront about on stage

BMW shipped their own experimental `funFactor` in the sample viewer, and it multiplies by distance ridden — so a square simply gets a higher "fun" score for having more road in it, regardless of quality. It's a popularity count hiding inside a quality score. We normalise everything per kilometre instead, and use rider count only as a *confidence* measure (few riders → trust the number less). Naming that difference out loud is the strongest possible signal that we actually read their data.
